title: Enterprise Prospect Playbook: Positioning, Competitive Briefs, Pitch Deck Guidance, Pricing, Case Studies & Security FAQ
author: Aisha Patel
body:
Summary:

This playbook is the canonical sales enablement reference for enterprise prospect conversations. It bundles: concise positioning & messaging, competitive battle cards, a recommended pitch-deck structure, pricing guidance and deal assembly tips, two short case studies with measurable outcomes, and a security FAQ tailored for technical buyers. Use this during discovery, technical validation, and commercial negotiation.

Audience:
- Enterprise AEs and Solutions Engineers
- GTM leadership (Sales, Presales, RevOps)
- Customer-facing Engineering resources

Owner and Escalation:
- Primary owner: Go-to-market (Aisha Patel)
- SE technical lead: Daniel Kim
- For legal/compliance questions: Security & Compliance (Maya Singh)

1) One-line and Elevator Positioning

One-line: Redwood Inference is a developer-first inference platform that makes high-performance, reliable LLM inference predictable and economical across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.

Elevator (30s):
- Problem: Companies struggle to deploy LLM features at scale because inference economics, latency, and reliability vary dramatically by model and hardware.
- Solution: Redwood provides a unified runtime + control plane that delivers consistent latency, automated batching & caching, and predictable cost controls across hosted, dedicated, and private modes.
- Why it matters: Teams get production-quality inference without operating complexity — results are repeatable across regions and compliant for regulated workloads.

2) Core Value Themes (talk tracks for discovery calls)

- Predictable economics: usage-based hosted pricing plus reserved capacity options for predictable unit costs.
- Production reliability: SLA-backed Dedicated offering, graceful fallbacks, per-route observability.
- Developer experience: one API for text, chat, embeddings and reranking; SDKs and quickstarts for <1 hour proof-of-concept.
- Deployment flexibility & compliance: VPC/private on-prem deployments with KMS/HSM integrations and audit logging.

3) Battle Card: Top Competitors & Differentiation (quick reference)

| Competitor | Typical customer ask | Redwood differentiation | Risk / Objection | Suggested response |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cloud provider managed endpoints | "We want one vendor for infra + model hosting" | Redwood focuses on inference runtime optimizations (batching, KV cache), model catalog with performance profiles, and predictable unit economics across clouds | Customer already committed to a cloud contract | Emphasize hybrid option: Redwood API + private deployment and marketplace integrations; show cost/latency benchmark for comparable workload |
| LLM API players (few-model, simple API) | "We want simple API and best model accuracy" | More production features: dedicated capacity, private deployment, rollout controls, and tooling for cost/quality tradeoffs | Perception of more complex product | Call out single SDK, quickstarts, and managed Starter plan for rapid PoC |
| Self-hosted inference stacks (open-source runtimes + infra) | "Control + cost savings" | Redwood provides same control with operational tooling, autoscaling, and SRE runbooks; reduces engineering time-to-production | Customer wants 100% control/on-prem | Offer Private deployment or on-prem package and joint runbook review; highlight support SLA and upgrade process |

Note: keep this slide to 1–2 rows for the competitor most relevant to prospect.

4) Common Objections and Scripts

- "We already have GPUs / infra": Ask about operational cost and engineering time required for runbook/rollouts. Position Redwood Dedicated as way to reduce ops burden while keeping control.
- "We can't expose data to a hosted API": Offer Redwood Private (VPC/on-prem) and discuss KMS/HSM & audit logging options.
- "Your unit economics vs our open-source stack": Request token/usage profile; run a benchmark using our perf suite and provide a formal cost comparison.

5) Recommended Pitch Deck Structure (10–12 slides for initial enterprise meeting)

1. Title & short intro (1 line value prop)
2. The problem we solve (customer pain + metrics)
3. Redwood solution overview (hosted, dedicated, private)
4. Architecture (high-level runtime + routing + caching)
5. Performance: latency & throughput benchmarks (by model/sequence length)
6. Cost controls & pricing model (illustrative example)
7. Reliability & SLAs (Dedicated + fallback policies)
8. Security & compliance summary (data residency, KMS, audit logs)
9. Case study / reference (similar industry)
10. Implementation plan & timeline (PoC -> pilot -> production)
11. Commercial ask (next steps & decision timeline)
12. Appendix (detailed benchmarks, integration checklist)

Slide guidance: use visuals (latency heatmaps, cost vs accuracy charts) and include a 1-slide appendix with CLI/SDK example for technical audiences.

6) Pricing Guidance and Deal Assembly Patterns

Pricing models (talk track):
- Hosted API: usage-based (per-token / per-embedding) with free trial credits for PoC.
- Dedicated: reserved capacity (monthly/annual commit) for predictable throughput and SLA; unit price lower than hosted for committed volume.
- Private: platform licensing + support/installation fee for on-prem or VPC; typical 12–36 month contract and volume-based pricing.

Commercial constructs we commonly use:
- PoC Offer: 1–4 weeks of free credits + technical support from SE; goal: validate latency and cost targets with 1–2 production prompts.
- Pilot: time-boxed pilot (30–90 days) on Dedicated or Hosted with capped spend and success criteria (SLOs and quality gates).
- Enterprise Contract: committed capacity + overage rates, optional premium SLA, and professional services for Private onboarding.

Pricing examples (illustrative only):
| Tier | Pricing model | Typical buyer | Contract |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Starter | Hosted, pay-as-you-go | SMB/Dev early PoC | Month-to-month |
| Business | Hosted + volume discounts | Growing SaaS teams | Annual with spend forecast |
| Dedicated | Reserved capacity | Product teams with steady traffic | 12–36 month commit |
| Private | License + services | Regulated enterprises | 12–36 months + SOW |

Deal velocity tips:
- Use a PoC as the primary close motion for technical buyers; aim for a 30–45 day PoC -> pilot cadence.
- Secure an executive sponsor early when selling Dedicated/Private (security or platform owner).
- Include a technical checklist in the SOW: network peering, KMS matrix, model pinning, rollout policy, and rollback plan.

7) Implementation & PoC Checklist (technical acceptance criteria)

Required for a successful PoC:
1. Define success criteria: latency 95p < X ms, cost per 1k tokens < $Y, output quality using evaluation prompt-set >= baseline.
2. Provide sample workload: 1–3 representative prompt types, typical sequence lengths, and QPS target.
3. Provide data residency needs and allowable logs (none/partial/full).
4. Identify infra preference: Hosted / Dedicated / Private.
5. Stakeholders: SE owner, infra owner, security/compliance reviewer.
6. Timeline: PoC kick, mid-point review, final evaluation.

8) Two Short Case Studies (1–2 paragraphs each; anonymized where required)

Case Study A — Fintech (Regulated, High Throughput)
- Situation: Fintech provider needed sub-200ms responses for document understanding workflows and strict data residency controls in EU.
- Solution: Private deployment in EU region + model caching and quantization profile recommended by Redwood Optimize.
- Outcome: 45% reduction in per-request compute cost, average latency 160ms (95p 240ms), and successful audit for data residency.

Case Study B — Large SaaS (Customer Support Automation)
- Situation: SaaS provider wanted to replace a rules-based routing system with an LLM-based assistant while keeping token cost predictable.
- Solution: Deploy Redwood Dedicated with automatic batching, KV prefix caching, and rollout-based canary.
- Outcome: 3x throughput improvement during peak windows, 30% lower cost per ticket compared to initial self-hosted benchmark, and a safe canary rollout that eliminated regressions.

9) Security FAQ for Prospects (technical answers for SEs)

Q: Where is customer data stored and how is it isolated?
A: Hosted API data is stored in region-specific storage; Dedicated instances maintain tenant isolation in separated GPU pools and network segments. Private deployments run entirely in customer VPC or on-prem per SOW. We provide architecture diagrams on request.

Q: Do you support KMS / BYOK / HSM?
A: Yes. Redwood supports cloud KMS integrations (AWS KMS, Google KMS, Azure Key Vault) and HSM-based BYOK for Private deployments.

Q: How do you handle logs and telemetry?
A: Audit logs are configurable. For Hosted we retain request-level metadata according to customer agreement; Dedicated and Private customers can opt into no retention for payloads and only store metrics. Logs can be shipped to customer SIEM via secure forwarders.

Q: What compliance regimes do you support?
A: We maintain SOC2 Type II and are actively pursuing ISO 27001 (contact Security for current evidence). For regulated workloads we recommend Private deployment + additional contractual terms (DPA, SCCs).

Q: How do you ensure model behavior & safety?
A: Redwood provides built-in eval tooling and quality guardrails. For enterprise customers we run prompt-set-based regression monitoring and can configure model variants, output filters, and fallback policies in the control plane.

Q: What is your incident communication process?
A: For Dedicated/Private customers we provide an incident runbook, SLA-based escalation, and a dedicated account channel. We map incidents to severity levels with defined MTTR targets and post-incident reviews.

- For new enterprise opportunities: attach this playbook to the opportunity in CRM and schedule a joint discovery with SE within 5 business days.
- Use the PoC checklist as part of the opportunity stage gate before pilot signature.
- When Dedicated/Private is being evaluated, request a security artifact pack from Security & Compliance and schedule a 60-minute architecture review.
